beats.headline: Why does Java distinguish between Errors and Exceptions?
beats.subline: It isn't just naming—it defines what your application can actually recover from.
beats.narration: Why does Java distinguish between Errors and Exceptions? It isn't just naming—it defines what your application can actually recover from. Let's decode the hierarchy.

beats.title: The Throwable Tree
beats.subtitle: Root -> Branch -> Leaf
beats.narration: The hierarchy starts at Throwable. Errors are fatal system failures like OutOfMemory. Checked Exceptions are external, recoverable events. RuntimeExceptions represent your own logic bugs.

beats.title: Checked vs. Unchecked

steps.explanation: Compiler forces you to handle or declare this.
Signals a contract violation; don't force callers to catch.

beats.narration: Checked exceptions force the caller to handle the failure. Unchecked exceptions are for contract violations—like negative ages—where catching is usually just noise.

beats.title: Catching Strategy
beats.narration: Avoid catching Errors. If the JVM hits an OutOfMemoryError, the state is already corrupted. Only catch what you can actually fix.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next: The hidden risks of finally blocks →
beats.narration: That's the hierarchy. In Part 2, we look at the try-catch-finally execution rules and why returning from finally is a dangerous bug.

beats.headline: Can a finally block hide an exception?
beats.subline: Yes, and it happens silently during return statements.
beats.narration: Can a finally block hide an exception? Yes, and it happens silently during return statements. It is one of the most common ways to lose root causes in production.

beats.title: The Finally Trap

steps.explanation: The state exception is thrown here.
The return here discards the exception entirely.

beats.narration: When you return from a finally block, the original exception is discarded. The caller receives 'true' and the error vanishes without a trace in your logs.

beats.title: Multi-Catch Syntax

top.label: Old Way
top.code:
catch (IO e) { log(e); }
catch (SQL e) { log(e); }

bottom.label: Java 7+

beats.narration: Use multi-catch for unrelated exceptions that share the same recovery logic. It keeps your handlers concise and prevents logic drift.

beats.title: Catch Ordering
beats.caption: Specific first, General last
beats.narration: Always order catches from most specific to most general. If you catch Exception first, the compiler will block you because the specific catch is unreachable.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
beats.narration: Finally blocks are for cleanup only. In Part 3, we see how try-with-resources handles suppressed exceptions to keep your stack traces clean.

beats.headline: What happens when both your code AND your close() fail?
beats.subline: Java's try-with-resources manages this with 'suppressed' exceptions.
beats.narration: What happens when both your code and your close method fail? Java's try-with-resources manages this with suppressed exceptions so you never lose the root cause.

beats.title: AutoCloseable Magic
beats.narration: When you use try-with-resources, the primary exception is preserved. Any failure during closing is attached as a suppressed exception, visible via getSuppressed.

beats.title: Reverse Order Cleanup
beats.subtitle: Closing sequence matters
beats.narration: Resources are closed in reverse order of declaration. This ensures wrappers flush their data before the underlying stream is destroyed.

beats.title: AutoCloseable vs Closeable
beats.narration: Closeable is for I/O streams. AutoCloseable is for everything else, like DB connections or custom locks. Use the most specific one available.

beats.narration: That's resource management. In Part 4, we discuss why throwing exceptions is expensive and how to design clean domain-specific error types.

beats.headline: Why is throwing an exception so slow?
beats.subline: It's not the try block—it's the stack trace generation.
beats.narration: Why is throwing an exception so slow? It's not the try block—it's the stack trace generation. Every throw walks the entire call stack.

beats.title: Bytecode Exception Table
beats.caption: The 'try' block is free!

lines.text: No branch instructions on happy path
Only used if an exception is thrown

beats.narration: The try block itself is free. The JVM uses an Exception Table to map code ranges to handlers. It only performs work if an exception actually occurs.

beats.title: Custom Domain Exceptions
beats.narration: Always chain the root cause in domain exceptions. This preserves the stack trace while hiding low-level implementation details from your business logic.

beats.title: Fast-Throw Optimization
beats.narration: HotSpot can omit stack traces for repeated exceptions to save time. If you see a bare NPE, check your JVM flags or log history.

beats.title: Chapter Complete
beats.narration: You've mastered Java exceptions. Checkout the branch for full labs and test your knowledge on the road map. See you in the next level.
